claim: The house style rests on the Chicago Manual of Style 16th ed. and Merriam-Webster's Collegiate 11th ed., with the guide covering only D&D-specific departures.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: The Chicago Manual of Style, 16th edition

verdict.trueWording: The Chicago Manual of Style, 16th edition
verdict.note: SUPERSEDED - verbatim in the v1.04a guide they cite; the 2019 v1.08a reverses the rule; cite as history only. R11 finding 2, re-ordered by the chair at 04:36 (r13 item 4; asked in r9, r10 and r12): CONTRADICTED is wrong for a rule that was true of its edition.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: none - the quoted Chicago-16th foundation is verbatim in v1.04a; the row is edition-bound, not false, and must carry the SUPERSEDED mark (v1.08a rests on Chicago 17th)

claim: Rules text is written in the second person, which the guide presents as the standard way to achieve gender neutrality; singular 'they' is banned outside dialogue and 'he/she' alternation is forbidden.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: achieve gender neutrality by writing in the second person

verdict.trueWording: In rules text, we often achieve gender neutrality by writing in the second person.
verdict.note: SUPERSEDED - verbatim in the v1.04a guide they cite; the 2019 v1.08a reverses the rule; cite as history only. R11 finding 2, re-ordered by the chair at 04:36 (r13 item 4; asked in r9, r10 and r12): CONTRADICTED is wrong for a rule that was true of its edition.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: none - the quoted second-person/gender-neutrality rule and the singular-'they' ban are verbatim in v1.04a; the row is edition-bound, not false, and must carry the SUPERSEDED mark (v1.08a allows singular 'they')

claim: 5e abandoned the 3E/4E use of 'result' for the number rolled and 4E's 'save' for a successful saving throw; 'magic item' never 'magical item'; 'deals 10 fire damage' not 'points of damage'; 'hit point maximum' not 'maximum hit points'.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: We have abandoned that practice.

verdict.trueWording: We have abandoned that practice.
verdict.note: The sentence appears twice, verbatim, once for each abandonment: under 'Saving Throws' ('In 4E, we used "save" as a synonym for "successful saving throw." We have abandoned that practice.') and under '"Result" and Die Rolls' ('In 3E and 4E, the word "result" was sometimes used as a synonym for "the number rolled on a die." We have abandoned that practice.'). Also confirmed: '"magic item" and its variants should never be "magical item"'; 'write, "The spell deals 10 fire damage," not "The spell deals 10 points of fire damage"'; 'When you write about a creature's hit point maximum, avoid "maximum hit points."'

feature: capitalisation and italics of game terms
claim: Ability scores, class features, skills, planes, feats and 'Dungeon Master' are capitalised; spells and magic items are italicised and treated as titles, distinct from the effects they create.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: The italicized terms are treated as titles

verdict.trueWording: The italicized terms are treated as titles, even when they don't use title capitalization.
verdict.note: 'Terms to Capitalize' lists Ability scores, Armor Class, Artifacts, Class features, Difficulty Class, Dungeon Master, Feats, Languages, Planes of existence, Skills, Traits. 'Terms to Italicize' lists Artifacts, Magic items, Spells. The distinctness point is verbatim: 'Don't confuse one of these titles with an effect it creates... the wall of fire spell produces a wall of fire, not a wall of fire.' Note artifacts are BOTH capitalized and italicized.

claim: American spelling, serial comma required, possessive 's' after names ending in s ('Asmodeus's'), 'non-' hyphenated before fantasy races ('non-elf') but 'nonhuman', 'not' contractions encouraged, vertical lists introduced by a full sentence and colon.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: We require the serial comma.

verdict.trueWording: We require the serial comma.
verdict.note: All six sub-claims confirmed verbatim: 'We use American style for spelling and punctuation'; the serial-comma sentence; 'We write "Asmodeus's lair," not "Asmodeus' lair"'; 'non-elf, non-dwarf, non-orc, non-drow (but nonhuman, as in Webster's)'; 'We encourage the use of contractions formed with "not"'; 'introduce it with a complete sentence ended by a colon' for vertical lists.

claim: Page references are avoided as error-prone; sections and sidebars are cited by quoted title and chapters by number.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: We avoid page references as much as possible.

verdict.trueWording: We avoid page references as much as possible.
verdict.note: Continues 'They are labor-intensive (they must be added by hand during galley review), and they invite error.' Cross-reference style confirmed: 'When you refer to a chapter, use its number' and 'When you refer to a subsection, including a sidebar, use its title in quotes.' One refinement: a table title is explicitly NOT enclosed in quotes.

claim: Dungeon magazine (Paizo era) required read-aloud text to be a bare-bones area description that never references the viewer or presumes player action, banning phrases like 'you see' and 'as you enter the room'.
source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
quote: it does not make any reference to the viewer

verdict.trueWording: Read-aloud text provides a bare-bones description of the encounter area; it does not make any reference to the viewer.
verdict.note: Verbatim on the page (page 12-13 boundary); my PDF text extractor merely dropped the space at the 'it / does' line break. Next sentence is verbatim too: 'Avoid phrases such as "you see," "as you enter the room," or other phrases that assume any action whatsoever on behalf of the players.' Paizo attribution confirmed by the document itself: byline 'By the DUNGEON Staff', address 'DUNGEON Magazine, Paizo Publishing, 2700 Richards Road, Suite 201, Bellevue, WA'. Era is 3.5e (cites Monster Manual II, Fiend Folio, Draconomicon, DUNGEON #114).

feature: read-aloud text: no creatures, few sentences
claim: Read-aloud text should exclude creatures (whose positions depend on circumstances) and only rarely run more than a few sentences; long descriptive passages belong in player handouts.
source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
quote: should only rarely run more than a few sentences

verdict.trueWording: Read-aloud text for an encounter should only rarely run more than a few sentences.
verdict.note: Both halves verbatim and adjacent: 'You should also avoid including descriptions of any creatures in the room, since their activities and positions in the room often depend on multiple factors (such as if they hear the PCs coming, if it's night or day, and so on).' and 'Long sections of read-aloud text are better served as player handouts.'

claim: Dungeon guidelines tell writers an adventure is not a short story, to condense backstory in favour of PC involvement, and never to presume PC actions or railroad.
source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
quote: an adventure is not a short story

verdict.trueWording: Regardless of how cool your backstory is, an adventure is not a short story.
verdict.note: Quote verbatim in the query-writing tips. Continues: 'You need to condense or sacrifice background description in favor of telling us about PC involvement. It's how the adventure PLAYS that determines whether or not a proposal is something we want to pick up.' The anti-railroad half is verbatim elsewhere: 'Avoid excessively linear plots that force the story toward an inevitable conclusion or "railroad" the actions of the PCs. The adventure should be flexible enough for PCs to make choices and decisions that could affect the outcome of the story. Avoid rigid timelines.' The design guide adds 'The Adventure Background section should be no more than 5% of the total length of the adventure.'

feature: boxed text length and person (official 5e guidance)
claim: D&D Beyond's official column advises boxed text of roughly four sentences under 100 words, phrased as third-person scene statements rather than 'as you enter, you notice', limited to perceivable sensory detail and excluding PC feelings, villain monologues and non-mechanical game terms.
source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond, 2019-11-06
quote: Read your boxed text aloud to check readability

verdict.trueWording: Tip 5. Read your boxed text aloud to check readability
verdict.note: Quote verbatim (Tip 5 heading). Every element confirmed on the page: 'Four sentences, and less than 100 words.'; third-person example replacing 'As you enter the clearing, you notice the bloated corpse of a headless dragon'; Tip 3 'Describe everything the characters can sense, but not what they can't'; boxed text criticised when it 'assumes a character's feelings, movements, actions, or reactions'; the four-paragraph villain 'boxed-text monologue' criticised; Tip 6 'Avoid game mechanical terms used in a non-mechanical way'. Byline 'by Shawn Merwin / Nov 6, 2019' matches. Fetched by WebFetch and re-fetched raw by curl (HTTP 200).

claim: Boxed text should describe only what characters perceive, treating everything sensed as 'appears to be' rather than asserting hidden facts.
source: Shawn Merwin, D&D Beyond, 2019-11-06
quote: Everything they sense 'appears to be' what it is

verdict.trueWording: Everything they sense “appears to be” what it is.
verdict.note: Word-for-word match; only the inner quotation marks differ (page uses curly double quotes, the claim renders them single). Full context: 'Tip 4. Avoid “seems to be” or “appears to be.” For the characters, perception is reality.' Supports the claim that boxed text should describe only what characters perceive without hedging.

claim: Chris Perkins says published adventure text should entertain the DM who reads it, seeding humour and Easter eggs so the DM is more inclined to run it, and hooks should appeal to 80–90% of players.
source: Todd Kenreck, 'Chris Perkins on Writing Your Own Adventures', D&D Beyond, 2018-04-19
quote: having had a few good laughs

verdict.trueWording: if they come away from reading that adventure, having had a few good laughs, they're much more inclined to run it
verdict.note: Quote verbatim, spoken by Chris Perkins. Also verbatim on the page: 'if you are going to make somebody read something for **** sakes', make it entertaining'; 'Put puns in your adventure. Put little laughs. Put little Easter eggs in your adventure.'; and 'the bait has to be something that is generally applicable ... maybe 80 or 90% of players are going to latch onto'. Byline 'by Todd Kenreck / Apr 19, 2018' matches. Note: the 80-90% line is about the adventure hook/bait, exactly as claimed.

claim: Boxed text is descriptive text in the adventure book meant to be read aloud verbatim or paraphrased, interleaved with rules references, and the DM-facing text explicitly instructs when to read or skip it.
source: Callison-Burch et al., 'Dungeons and Dragons as a Dialogue Challenge for AI', EMNLP 2022, Appendix B
quote: Read the boxed text when you're ready to start.

verdict.trueWording: Read the boxed text when you’re ready to start.
verdict.note: Quote verbatim (curly apostrophe) inside Appendix B, 'B Lost Mine of Phadelver Adventure', of the EMNLP 2022 paper (Callison-Burch, Tomar, Martin, Ippolito et al.). The definition is also verbatim: 'The adventure book provides boxed text, which is descriptive text to be read aloud verbatim or to paraphrase. It also gives details about the combat ... and links to relevant [rules]'; and the skip instruction follows: 'If you create a different adventure hook, skip to the second paragraph'. Paper title is 'Dialog Challenge', not 'Dialogue Challenge' — trivial. Verified by extracting the PDF text locally (15 pages).

feature: DM preference for boxed text (designer poll)
claim: A Jeremy Crawford Twitter poll cited by McKenzie found 59.5% of DMs prefer occasional boxed text, 34.4% want lots, and about 6% want none.
source: Brian McKenzie, Analog Game Studies, 2023-12-18
quote: occasional boxed text

verdict.trueWording: The results were 59.5% desired “occasional boxed text,” 34.4% “lots of boxed text,” and only 6% of respondents did not want any boxed text.
verdict.note: All three figures and the phrase 'occasional boxed text' verbatim. Attribution confirmed: 'A Twitter poll by D&D's current lead rules designer Jeremy Crawford saw 2,248 replies to the question “How much boxed text (aka read-aloud text) do you like in an adventure you run?”' (endnote 38 cites @JeremyECrawford, 17 Nov 2016). The claim's 'about 6%' matches 'only 6%'.

feature: read-aloud text function and NPC action
claim: Grouling Cover describes module read-aloud text as passages the DM is instructed to read that usually describe location but sometimes narrate NPC action, and likens it to a videogame cut-scene.
source: Jennifer Grouling Cover, The Creation of Narrative in Tabletop Role-Playing Games (McFarland 2010), pp. 64–66, 80
quote: read aloud text that the DM is instructed to read

verdict.trueWording: read aloud text that the DM is instructed to read to the players. Often these passages describe the location, but sometimes they are also used to describe the action of NPCs
verdict.note: Google Books snippet for p.64 of Cover's book carries the quoted fragment word for word plus the location/NPC-action distinction. The cut-scene comparison is on the adjacent snippets: p.65 '... read aloud in the TRPG, but add more visual interest. Cut-scenes are moments in a videogames where the gameplay is interrupted by a visual scene' and p.66 '... read aloud text in the module. The opening of the computer game is a fairly elaborate cut-scene'. Cited pages 64-66 and 80 all return snippets. Route note: WebFetch of the URL returned metadata only; the snippets came from the same URL fetched raw with curl (HTTP 200), whose embedded JSON holds four search_results.

claim: Monte Cook characterises AD&D's house voice as heavy passive voice, stream-of-consciousness digressions, an advanced vocabulary and an authoritative, treatise-like tone that legitimised the hobby.
source: Monte Cook, 'How you say it', Substack, 2021-07-27
quote: the passive voice a lot, the occasional stream-of-consciousness digressions

verdict.trueWording: using the passive voice a lot, the occasional stream-of-consciousness digressions
verdict.note: Live fetch 200. Quote is word for word in Cook's own sentence, which continues 'an advanced vocabulary (I was a 14-year-old who used terms like "weal or woe" because of Gary), and a very authoritative tone.' The treatise/legitimacy element is also explicit: 'Reading Gary's AD&D Dungeon Master's Guide was like reading a treatise on some vital topic of complexity and depth' and 'it was meaningful to read someone treating the activity we loved as seriously as a scholar would' / 'We felt that it was both validating and compelling.' Claim fully supported.

claim: Stu Horvath (MIT Press, 2023) calls the 1979 DMG strange and deeply idiosyncratic, a singular authorial vision; Wieck (1989) says the 2e DMG became as much advice as manual; Taylor notes the 5e DMG spends 127 pages teaching a novice DM.
source: Wikipedia, 'Dungeon Master's Guide' (citing Horvath 2023, Wieck 1989, Taylor/Black Gate)
quote: strange and deeply idiosyncratic

verdict.trueWording: The Dungeon Master's Guide is strange and deeply idiosyncratic
verdict.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. Quote word for word inside the Horvath quotation, cited to Monsters, Aliens, and Holes in the Ground (MIT Press, 2023, p. 58); continues 'Gygax expresses in it a singular vision that feels true'. Wieck element verbatim: 'it has become as much a guide of advice for Dungeon Masters as a manual of specific information' (White Wolf #17, 1989). Taylor element verbatim: 'The 5E DMG devotes the first 127 pages to teaching a novice player how to [be] a Dungeon Master in this system' (Black Gate). All three sub-claims supported.

claim: Wikipedia's PHB synthesis records Turnbull (1978) calling OD&D 'ambiguous and muddled' against the coherent AD&D PHB, Schick (1991) on 2e spell descriptions bloating past 100 pages, Kelly (2014) on more polished writing, and Abbott (2024) on the 2014 spell chapter as a wall of text.
source: Wikipedia, 'Player's Handbook'
quote: an unrelenting wall of text

verdict.trueWording: the spell section was an unrelenting wall of text
verdict.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. Quote word for word (Benjamin Abbott, GamesRadar+, August 20 2024, about the 2014 edition). Turnbull element verbatim: 'whereas the original rules are ambiguous and muddled, the Handbook is a detailed and coherent game-system, and very sophisticated' - but the ref dates that review White Dwarf #10, December 1978 - January 1979, so '(1978)' is only approximately right. Schick element verbatim: spell descriptions 'have positively bloated to over 100 pages' (Heroic Worlds, 1991). Kelly element verbatim: 'the writing is much more polished' (GeekDad, August 18 2014). All four sub-claims supported.

claim: Games scholar Jaroslav Švelch sees the Monster Manual as modelled on medieval bestiaries but with precise figures; Turnbull praised its explanatory text for amplifying the statistics.
source: Wikipedia, 'Monster Manual' (citing Švelch, Turnbull)
quote: medieval bestiaries, only with more precise figures

verdict.trueWording: modeled after medieval bestiaries, only with more precise figures
verdict.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. Quote word for word: 'Games scholar Jaroslav Svelch saw the Monster Manual modeled after "medieval bestiaries, only with more precise figures"' (Monster Culture in the 21st Century, Bloomsbury, 2013, p. 197). Turnbull element verbatim: he 'praised the explanatory text, stating that it "amplifies, where necessary, [the game statistics] and the result is the most comprehensive listing of D&D monsters you will find"' (White Dwarf #8, Aug-Sep 1978). Both sub-claims supported.

claim: Kunzelman (Paste) reads Volo's authorship as a deliberate device letting the sourcebook include rumor and error, and Furniss praises its marriage of narrative and mechanical information.
source: Wikipedia, 'Volo's Guide to Monsters' (citing Kunzelman, Furniss)
quote: having Volo write the guide means that he can be wrong

verdict.trueWording: having Volo write the guide means that he can be wrong
verdict.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. Quote word for word (the source has wiki italic markup around 'wrong', which renders identically). Kunzelman/Paste element supported: 'Volo is a device through which the designers of the Forgotten Realms can give Dungeon Masters a set of bounds ... Whatever Volo thinks or writes can be slightly off the mark'; the 'rumor and error' framing is explicit in his later review, which faults the book because it 'mostly tells the DM facts about a world, rather than opinions, rumors and suspicions that might be completely unfounded'. Furniss element verbatim: 'I love the marriage of narrative and mechanical information' (Destructoid, 16 November 2016).

claim: A GeekDad reviewer cited on Wikipedia says reading Curse of Strahd front to back is like reading a choose-your-own-adventure book, and Black Gate calls it a setting manual and adventure in one.
source: Wikipedia, 'Curse of Strahd' (citing Bristol, Jones)
quote: like reading a choose-your-own-adventure book front to back

verdict.trueWording: like reading a choose-your-own-adventure book from front to back
verdict.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. NOT verbatim: the claim's quote drops 'from'. The page reads 'it was a bit like reading a choose-your-own-adventure book from front to back, rather than following the breadcrumbs' (Rory Bristol, GeekDad, 2016-03-15). Substance otherwise supported, including the second element verbatim: Andrew Zimmerman Jones in Black Gate said Curse of Strahd 'is really a mix of setting manual and adventure module in one'.

claim: Evan Torner, cited on Wikipedia, describes 3e's design intent as Eurogame-style elegance in which terminology and choices should be immediately intelligible.
source: Wikipedia, 'Editions of Dungeons & Dragons' (citing Torner)
quote: immediately intelligible to all who might play it

verdict.trueWording: terminology and choices should be immediately intelligible to all
verdict.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. Quote word for word inside Torner's sentence: 'D&D 3e and 3.5e bear the influence of Eurogame-style elegant design: that the terminology and choices in the game should be immediately intelligible to all who might play it', with the designers' aim given as to 'simplify and declutter the whole system'. Cited to Evan Torner, 'Combat In Dungeons & Dragons', Fifty Years of Dungeons & Dragons (MIT Press, 2024). Claim fully supported.

claim: Rhodes argues the 2014 PHB left DMs to guess whether words were ordinary or mechanical, and that the 2024 PHB fixes this by capitalising game mechanics and adding an A–Z Rules Glossary.
source: Duncan Rhodes, Hipsters & Dragons, 2025-03-10
quote: just being used in their normal sense

verdict.trueWording: just being used in their normal sense
verdict.note: Live site refused with HTTP 403; verified through the Wayback Machine snapshot 20251219191134 of the same URL. Quote word for word under heading '8. Capitalising Game Mechanics In The Text': 'It really is a crime that the 2014 Player's Handbook left DMs to work out if certain words were just being used in their normal sense or if they referred to some mechanic in the game. Thankfully that mistake wasn't repeated in 2024.' Glossary element supported under '2. Handy Rules Glossary': 'a dedicated rules glossary covering basically everything you need in an a-z of mechanics at the back of the book'. All three sub-claims supported.

claim: The official 2024 PHB update renames race to species, 'Cast a Spell action' to 'Magic action', Inspiration to 'Heroic Inspiration', 'Use an Object' to 'Utilize action', folds shoving into Unarmed Strike, and adds glossary entries such as Ally, Enemy, Bloodied and Passive Perception.
source: D&D Beyond staff, 'Updates in the Player's Handbook (2024)', 2024-09-03
quote: Magic action

verdict.trueWording: Cast a Spell action -> Magic action
verdict.note: Live fetch 200. 'Magic action' word for word in the Updated Terminology table, which also carries every other rename in the claim: Race -> Species, Cast a Spell action -> Magic action, Inspiration -> Heroic Inspiration, Use an Object action -> Utilize action, and Shoving -> Unarmed Strike. The 'New Rules' list of the 2024 Rules Glossary includes Ally, Bloodied, Enemy and Passive Perception (the glossary spells the action entry 'Magic (action)'). All sub-claims supported.

claim: Screen Rant notes the 2024 Rules Glossary de-emphasises art with monochrome scenes to prioritise text and lacks a dedicated Conditions section.
source: Ben Brosofsky, Screen Rant, 2024-09-21
quote: the lack of a dedicated section for Conditions

verdict.trueWording: the lack of a dedicated section for Conditions

The art clause is also verbatim on the page: 'the Rules Glossary is also the one part of DnD's 2024 Player's Handbook that largely de-emphasizes artwork, squeezing monochrome scenes into banners at the top of some pages but devoting most of the real estate to the text.' Both halves of the claim confirmed. Fetched via WebFetch, HTTP 200.

claim: Arndt reports the 2025 Monster Manual cuts iconic monsters' multi-page lore to at most three paragraphs and a roll table, adds a subtitle epithet to every monster, renames phylactery to 'spirit jar', and reads as a utilitarian encyclopedia.
source: Dan Arndt, The Fandomentals, 2025-01-28
quote: three paragraphs and a table to roll on

verdict.trueWording: three paragraphs and a table to roll on
verdict.note: Quote verbatim: 'Creatures like Aboleths, Beholders, and Mind Flayers from multi-page descriptions that show you their backstory and place in the world to, at best, three paragraphs and a table to roll on.' All three remaining sub-assertions confirmed on the page: subtitles — 'they also all now have Dark Souls boss subtitles' (article's word is 'subtitles', not 'epithet'); phylactery — 'Instead of the Greek word Phylactery ... the Monster Manual now uses "spirit jar."'; utilitarian encyclopedia — 'It goes from an in-universe collection of monster lore to a glorified encyclopedia. It's stripped down to something purely utilitarian.' Byline and date in page JSON-LD match the citation exactly: author 'Dan Arndt', datePublished 2025-01-28. WebFetch returned HTTP 403; retrieved via curl with a browser user agent, HTTP 200, 289,672 bytes.

claim: A written WotC house style guide exists — 'D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing' v1.04a (©2013), built on Chicago 16 and Merriam-Webster 11 — and it governs typography, numerals, verb collocations, capitalization and tone, with no rule at all on boxed/read-aloud text.
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
quote: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing

verdict.trueWording: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing; Version 1.04a ©2013
verdict.note: Raw PDF fetched (HTTP 200, 9 pp., pypdf extraction). p.1 carries the title verbatim, 'Version 1.04a ©2013 Wizards of the Coast', and the two named foundations: 'The Chicago Manual of Style, 16th edition' and 'Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary, 11th edition'. Governance limbs all present: typography ('Typographic Treatment of Product Names'), numerals ('Numerals versus Words', 'Numerals in Rules Text'), verb collocations ('Verb Usage', p.6), capitalization ('Terms to Capitalize', p.5), tone (the 'High Fantasy' sidebar: humor/tragedy must not 'overtake the general tone'). Boxed/read-aloud limb confirmed by absence: case-insensitive grep for 'box' = 0 hits and 'aloud' = 0 hits across all 9 pages.

claim: A later revision, v1.08a (©2018, circulated as 'updated January 2019'), keeps the same structure (Chicago 17 now) and adds headings hierarchy, sidebar, gender-suffix, 'fellowship vs party' and edition-naming rules; it still contains nothing on boxed text or read-aloud prose.
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)
quote: Avoid overusing sidebars.

verdict.trueWording: Avoid overusing sidebars.
verdict.note: Raw PDF fetched (HTTP 200, 11 pp.). Quote appears verbatim as the opening of the new 'Sidebars' section (p.3). 'Version 1.08a ©2018 Wizards of the Coast' on every page; 'The Chicago Manual of Style, 17th edition' p.1. Additions confirmed against the v1.04a text: 'Headings' hierarchy section (Chapter Title / Heading 1-3 / Inline Subhead), 'Sidebars', 'Gender-Specific Suffixes', and 'Adventuring Parties' — which is the fellowship-vs-party rule ('The word “fellowship” has strong connections with The Lord of the Rings… use “group,” “band,” “company,” or, especially, “party.”'; 'fellowship' = 0 hits in v1.04a). Edition-naming rule is new in wording: 'In a departure from previous usage, we spell out and lowercase references to editions'. Boxed-text limb confirmed by absence: 'box' = 0 hits, 'aloud' = 0 hits. One nuance: 'updated January 2019' is the mirror's filename only — neither 'January' nor '2019' appears anywhere in the document — which matches the claim's own wording 'circulated as'.

Note for the record that the claim's url field holds only the first of the three; the other two limbs are verified on the pages the sentence itself names, not on half-cover.com.

claim: The official Adventurers League Dungeoncraft guide tells authors they must use the provided template and 'formatting standards as presented in the template' and be familiar with the D&D Style Guide, which it says is also provided.
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Adventurers League Dungeoncraft Design Guide: The Wild Beyond the Witchlight, v1.2 (media.wizards.com)
quote: You should be familiar with the D&D Style Guide

verdict.trueWording: You should be familiar with the D&D Style Guide (also provided) as well.
verdict.note: Raw PDF fetched from media.wizards.com (HTTP 200, 10 pp.). p.1 'TECHNICAL INFORMATION': 'A template is provided for use, including the Community Created D&D Adventurers League logo. You must use this template, and follow the formatting standards as presented in the template. This logo must appear on your adventure… You should be familiar with the D&D Style Guide (also provided) as well.' Both quoted fragments are verbatim, and 'also provided' carries the claim's final limb. The document self-identifies as 'Dungeoncraft Adventures: The Wild Beyond the Witchlight' for 'D&D Adventurers League' with 'Effective Date: October 1, 2021. Version 1.2.' The same passage repeats for the second option later in the document.

claim: The 2023 Dungeoncraft Design Guide (effective 2023-11-09) again requires a specific template and familiarity with the D&D Style Guide; a poster frames this as organized play needing 'more guiderails than your usual table does'.
source: EN World — D&D Adventurers League Unveils New DungeonCraft Document with Planescape In Focus (Raddu, 2023-11)
quote: more guiderails than your usual table does

verdict.trueWording: more guiderails than your usual table does
verdict.note: Raw thread fetched (HTTP 200; thread starter Raddu, Nov 13 2023). Article body: 'The newly released Dungeoncraft Design Guide, effective from November 9th, 2023, provides comprehensive instructions and standards for crafting these adventures' and 'Creators must use a specific template provided for Dungeoncraft adventures, including the Community Created D&D Adventurers League logo. Familiarity with the D&D Style Guide and adherence to the DMsGuild Content Guidelines are also required.' The forum quote is verbatim in a reply defending the requirements: 'These guidelines above, however, are part of style of play that needs more guiderails than your usual table does', in a post that frames the contrast as Adventurers League / Living campaign play versus a home table — matching 'a poster frames this as organized play'.

claim: The guide's stated reason for second person in rules text is gender neutrality: 'In rules text, we often achieve gender neutrality by writing in the second person.'
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
quote: writing in the second person

verdict.trueWording: In rules text, we often achieve gender neutrality by writing in the second person.
verdict.note: Raw PDF, p.2, under 'Gender' → 'Achieving Gender Neutrality'. The sentence appears exactly as the claim renders it, and it is the guide's only statement about second person, so 'the guide's stated reason for second person in rules text is gender neutrality' is precisely what the page says. (v1.08a softens the same rule to 'we prefer to achieve gender neutrality by writing in the second person whenever possible'.)

claim: The guide fixes the game's verb idiom in a list: you cast a spell, deal damage, make a saving throw that succeeds or fails, make an attack that hits or misses, take damage, regain hit points, score a critical hit, use a feature.
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
quote: You make a saving throw, and it succeeds or fails

verdict.trueWording: You make a saving throw, and it succeeds or fails.
verdict.note: Raw PDF p.6, 'Verb Usage' list. Every collocation in the claim is a line of that list, verbatim: 'You cast a spell.' / 'You deal damage.' / 'You make a saving throw, and it succeeds or fails.' / 'You make an attack (or you attack), and your attack hits or misses (it doesn't succeed or fail).' / 'You take damage.' / 'You regain hit points.' / 'You score a critical hit.' / 'You use a feature.' The list is indeed a fixed list of the game's verb idiom, so the framing limb holds as well.

claim: Common Pitfalls: never write 'must make a DC 15 Strength check' unless success and failure are described next; the canonical form is 'must succeed on'.
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
quote: You must succeed on a DC 15 Strength check

verdict.trueWording: You must succeed on a DC 15 Strength check to clamber up the wall.
verdict.note: Raw PDF p.6, 'Common Pitfalls' → 'Making a Roll vs. Succeeding on One', verbatim: 'Don't mistake making an ability check, a saving throw, or other roll with succeeding on it. The following sentence gets it right: “You must succeed on a DC 15 Strength check to clamber up the wall.” Don't write, “You must make a DC 15 Strength check to clamber up the wall,” unless that sentence is immediately followed by a description of what happens on a success or failure.' Both limbs — the prohibition-unless-consequences-follow and 'must succeed on' as the canonical form — are on the page, in the Common Pitfalls section the claim names.

claim: Third-party style guidance derived from the WotC guide: skill checks are always written as '[Ability Score] ([Skill])', outcomes are stated for success and failure, and multi-skill checks name at most two skills for brevity.
source: Kobold Press — Designing with Style: Ability Checks and Saving Throws (Hannah Rose, 2019-05-31)
quote: always written as [Ability Score] ([Skill])

verdict.trueWording: skill checks are always written as [Ability Score] ([Skill])
verdict.note: Raw HTML fetched (200, 529KB). Quote verbatim. All three limbs on page: the [Ability Score] ([Skill]) rule; success/failure outcome language (Option 1/Option 2, 'On a success... On a failure...'); and 'If there are more than two possible skills... you probably want to pick at most two for the sake of brevity and elegance.' Third-party derivation limb confirmed: 'The Designing with Style series breaks down the official 5th-edition style guide.' Byline Hannah Rose, May 31, 2019, both on page.

feature: numerals in rules vs words in narrative
claim: Rules text uses numerals for any game quantity ('regains 3 hit points', 'lasts for 1 round', 'The room is 20 feet square') while narrative time and distance are spelled out ('slept for six hours', 'fifty miles apart').
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
quote: the characters slept for six hours
page: v1.04a pp.5-6, Numerals in Rules Text

verdict.trueWording: After winning the fight, the characters slept for six hours.
verdict.note: PDF fetched (200, 1.24MB) and text-extracted with pypdf; 9 pages read in full. Quote verbatim on p.5 (line-broken in the PDF, contiguous when whitespace-normalized). Every example in the claim is verbatim in 'Numerals in Rules Text' (pp.5-6): 'Anyone who touches the orb regains 3 hit points.'; 'The spell lasts for 1 round.'; 'The room is 20 feet square.'; and under 'But:' — 'the characters slept for six hours' and 'The two cities are fifty miles apart.' Page citation pp.5-6 is correct.

claim: The guide explicitly retires 4e usages: 'save' as 'successful saving throw' and 'result' as 'the number rolled on a die' — 'We have abandoned that practice.'
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
quote: We have abandoned that practice

verdict.trueWording: In 4E, we used "save" as a synonym for "successful saving throw." We have abandoned that practice.
verdict.note: Quote 'We have abandoned that practice' appears verbatim TWICE on p.6, once in each named place. Minor precision point, not an unsupported limb: the guide attributes the 'result' usage to '3E and 4E', not 4E alone — 'In 3E and 4E, the word "result" was sometimes used as a synonym for "the number rolled on a die."' The 'save' usage is attributed to 4E alone, as claimed.

claim: Write 'deals 10 fire damage', not '10 points of fire damage'; write 'hit point maximum', not 'maximum hit points'; 'magic item' is never 'magical item'.
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
quote: Avoid referring to points of damage

verdict.trueWording: Avoid referring to points of damage. ... And "magic item" and its variants should never be "magical item."
verdict.note: All three limbs verbatim. p.6 'Points of Damage': 'write, "The spell deals 10 fire damage," not "The spell deals 10 points of fire damage."'; p.7 'Hit Point Maximum': 'When you write about a creature's hit point maximum, avoid "maximum hit points."'; p.6 '"Magic" vs. "Magical"': '"magic item" and its variants should never be "magical item."' Page citation pp.6-7 is correct.

claim: Capitalize ability scores, Armor Class, class features, Difficulty Class, feats, languages, planes, skills, racial/monster traits; italicize spell and magic-item names as titles (the spell wall of fire produces a wall of fire).
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)

verdict.trueWording: the wall of fire spell produces a wall of fire
verdict.note: Claim carries no quote field, and its parenthetical inverts the guide's word order (guide: 'the wall of fire spell produces a wall of fire'; claim: 'the spell wall of fire produces a wall of fire') — hence SUBSTANCE, not VERBATIM. Every listed term is on p.5 'Formatting Game Terms': Terms to Capitalize lists Ability scores, Armor Class, Artifacts, Class features, Difficulty Class, Dungeon Master, Feats, Languages, Planes of existence, Skills, 'Traits in races and monsters'; Terms to Italicize lists Artifacts, Magic items, Spells; and 'The italicized terms are treated as titles, even when they don't use title capitalization.'

claim: The only tone guidance in the guide: D&D is high fantasy about small teams; humor or tragedy is fine if it doesn't overtake the tone, tested against Lord of the Rings / Game of Thrones — 'ring wraiths aren't used for gags'.
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
quote: ring wraiths aren't used for gags

verdict.trueWording: there are moments of humor with the hobbits, but ring wraiths aren't used for gags
verdict.note: Quote verbatim on p.5, section 'High Fantasy'. Limbs verbatim: 'A typical D&D story or adventure is part of the high fantasy subgenre'; 'D&D is about small bands of characters embarking on adventures together'; 'Elements of humor or tragedy are fine, so long as they are true to the facts of the brand and don't overtake the general tone'; 'When in doubt, think about properties like the Lord of the Rings or Game of Thrones.' The 'only tone guidance' limb was checked exhaustively against all 9 pages: 'High Fantasy' is the sole section addressing narrative tone; the only other occurrence of 'tone' is the blog-register aside under '"Dungeon Master" Isn't a Verb'.

claim: v1.08a switches from '5th Edition' to lowercase 'fifth edition', preferably as a modifier ('the fifth edition Dungeon Master's Guide').
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)

verdict.trueWording: We write "fifth edition," for instance, not "5th Edition."
verdict.note: Claim carries no quote field, but all three of its inline quoted strings are verbatim on pp.1-2: 'In a departure from previous usage, we spell out and lowercase references to editions of the roleplaying game. We write "fifth edition," for instance, not "5th Edition." We prefer to use an edition designation as a modifier of another term—"the fifth edition Dungeon Master's Guide," for example.' The 'switches' limb is machine-confirmed by diff: v1.04a contains '5th Edition' and not 'fifth edition' (its edition list reads '1st Edition ... 5th Edition'); v1.08a's list reads 'first edition ... fifth edition'.

claim: v1.08a requires descending the heading hierarchy without skipping levels, forbids inline subheads used merely for emphasis, and says the best sidebars 'can appear anywhere on a page and still make sense'.
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)

verdict.trueWording: The best sidebars can appear anywhere on a page and still make sense.
verdict.note: The claim's inline quotation is verbatim on p.3. Limbs verbatim: 'Work your way down the heading hierarchy without skipping steps'; 'don't use an inline subhead when you simply want to emphasize a word or phrase. Use bold for such emphasis'. All three rules are new in v1.08a (v1.04a has no Headings or Sidebars section; 'skipping steps' and 'sidebars' are absent from it). Minor citation drift, not a limb: all three passages sit on p.3, not pp.3-4.

claim: Half-Cover infers from the books that spells and saving throws use 'very specific wording' and that features always spell out interactions (e.g., already having a cantrip), with fixed section order (starting equipment before class features).
source: Half-Cover — How to Follow the Writing Style of D&D (Michael, 2017-09-02)
quote: a strict style guide that all D&D sections adhere to

verdict.trueWording: a strict style guide that all D&D sections adhere to when explaining mechanics
verdict.note: Raw HTML fetched (200, 60KB). Quote verbatim. All limbs verbatim: 'This is why spells or saving throws have very specific wording'; 'the feature will always clarify what happens if you already have the cantrip because of another mechanic or feature in the game'; 'For example, starting equipment is always before class features in any class section.' The 'infers from the books' limb is supported: 'to my knowledge Wizards of the Coast has not yet published the official style guide for D&D 5th Edition' and 'the best way to draft your homebrew is to inspect the actual manuals'. Byline Michael, 2 Sep 2017, on page.

claim: In 2024 text, Bonus Action, Advantage/Disadvantage, Hit Points, Armor Class, Death Saving Throw, Proficiency Bonus, Challenge Rating and D20 Test are capitalized while ability, action, saving throw, skill, spell and feat stay lowercase; monster-name capitalization is inconsistent.
source: Blog of Holding — Unofficial D&D 2024 Style Guide (Paul Hughes, 2025-01-07)

verdict.trueWording: Capitalized list includes Bonus Action, D20 Test; not capitalized includes feat
verdict.note: Raw page read via curl. All eight capitalized terms appear verbatim in the 'Capitalized:' list (Advantage/Disadvantage, Armor Class, Bonus Action, Challenge Rating, D20 Test, Death Saving Throw, Hit Points, Proficiency Bonus). All six lowercase terms appear verbatim in the 'Not Capitalized:' list (ability, action, saving throw, skill, spell, feat). Monster-name inconsistency verbatim: 'monster name ("skeleton") (or perhaps its "Skeleton", it's inconsistent)'. Claim carried no quote field; every named term is literal.

claim: 2024 condition text is standardized to mechanical statements — 'Your Speed is 0 and can't increase' replaces 2014's 'can't move' — and 'Utilize', 'Study', 'Influence' and 'D20 Test' become defined capitalized terms.
source: Dungeon Master Assistance — D&D 5.5 PHB Review: Playing the Game and the Rules Glossary (Ronny, 2024-10-01)
quote: Your Speed is 0 and can't increase

verdict.trueWording: Your Speed is 0 and can't increase
verdict.note: Raw page read via curl. Quote verbatim: 'Any condition that had "can't move", was changed to "Your Speed is 0 and can't increase."' Standardization further supported by 'can't speak' being consolidated into Incapacitated. INFLUENCE and STUDY each flagged '(This is a new action.)'; UTILIZE 'is a renaming of the old "Use an Object" action'; 'D20 TEST: This is a simple new definition that they have added.' Capitalization of the action names is shown by the page's own usage (e.g. 'now called D20 Tests', 'Heavily Obscured', 'Hide check') and its all-caps headings rather than asserted outright.

feature: Curse of Strahd vs Storm King's Thunder boxed text
claim: DMDavid observes Perkins boxed every location in Curse of Strahd, even empty rooms, and that his next adventure, Storm King's Thunder, 'omits almost all read-aloud text' — the two extremes of WotC 5e practice.
source: DMDavid — How much description should a dungeon key include? (David Hartlage, 2016-11-21)
quote: omits almost all read-aloud text

verdict.trueWording: His follow-up, Storm King's Thunder, omits almost all read-aloud text
verdict.note: Raw page read via curl (post by David Hartlage, November 21, 2016, served on the tag archive URL). Verbatim: 'Curse of Strahd includes it for every location.'; 'DMs who dutifully present the box text for all the empty rooms in a place like the Argynvostholt dungeon will bore players.'; 'His follow-up, Storm King's Thunder, omits almost all read-aloud text. Find a happy middle, Chris.' The 'two extremes' framing is the claim's own wording but is carried by 'Find a happy middle' (and a commenter's 'On the other end of the spectrum, I find Storm King's Thunder barren').

claim: Every 2025 MM entry opens with a single characterizing phrase ('tentacled subterranean trapper', 'guardian manifestation of the divine'); lore is 'compact but effective' though 'a little too compact for my taste'; quote boxes appear on some entries.
source: EN World — Monsters & More: An In-Depth Review of the 2025 D&D Monster Manual (Beth Rimmels, 2025-01-28)
quote: tentacled subterranean trapper

verdict.trueWording: the Couatl is 'guardian manifestation of the divine' and the Roper 'tentacled subterranean trapper'
verdict.note: Raw page read via curl (EN World review by Beth Rimmels / brimmels, Jan 28 2025). Verbatim: 'every entry starts with a single phrase that gives the DM an efficient characterization of the creature. So the Couatl is "guardian manifestation of the divine" and the Roper is a "tentacled subterranean trapper."' Lore limbs verbatim in two places: 'The lore/background material is compact - a little too compact for my taste' and 'Narrative/lore material is compact but effective.' Quote boxes limb verbatim: 'Quote boxes are another way the new MM adds a bit more flavor and insight. Not every entry gets them'.

claim: TheGamer: 'The flavor has amped up narratively, and the mechanics have followed' (angels wield light, kenku use shadow-magic daggers); there is no lore glossary.
source: TheGamer — 2025 Monster Manual Review (Jerel Levy, 2025-01-28)

verdict.trueWording: The flavor has amped up narratively, and the mechanics have followed
verdict.note: Raw page read via curl (TheGamer, Jerel Levy, Published Jan 28 2025). Verbatim: 'The flavor has amped up narratively, and the mechanics have followed.' Angel example verbatim: 'where an angel might have been wielding a greatsword in the past... it now wields light itself in combat'. Kenku verbatim: 'The Kenku, known for being from the Shadowfell, now have a dagger with shadow magic.' No-lore-glossary limb verbatim: 'Though there is no lore glossary similar to what the Dungeon Master's Guide has'. Claim carried no quote field; the sentence it paraphrases is literal on the page.

claim: Xanathar's Guide carries 'little notes that run as commentary throughout the book, usually a sort of joke or snipe about the subject matter', continuing the Volo's device but less relevant on a mechanics-heavy book.
source: Skyland Games — Review: Xanathar's Guide to Everything (Scott D, 2017-11-13)
quote: a sort of joke or snipe about the subject matter

verdict.trueWording: little notes that run as commentary throughout the book, usually a joke
verdict.note: Raw page read via curl (Skyland Games, Scott D, November 13, 2017). Whole claim verbatim in one sentence pair: 'As with Volo's Guide to Monsters, there are little notes that run as commentary throughout the book, usually a sort of joke or snipe about the subject matter. As the material is largely mechanics and game lore, it's less relevant than with Volo's but still fun.' Every limb - the device, the Volo's lineage, and the reduced relevance on a mechanics-heavy book - is on the page.

claim: Dyson Logos, citing Decker and Noonan's 2005 GenCon table observations, holds that a DM gets two sentences before players stack dice; players missed dimensions, exits and monster counts in longer boxed text.
source: Dyson's Dodecahedron — The Dreaded Boxed Text (Dyson Logos, 2013-09-29)
quote: you get two sentences. Period.

verdict.trueWording: If you're the DM, you get two sentences. Period.
verdict.note: Raw page via Wayback id_ capture 20210728094635 (live host 403s a bot UA). Page carries verbatim: 'If you're the DM, you get two sentences. Period. Beyond that, your players are stacking dice, talking to each other, or staring off into space' and 'missing the actual data in the boxed text - basic stuff, like room dimensions, how many doors exit the room, and number of monsters.' Dyson explicitly frames it as 'Back in 2005 when Jesse Decker and David Noonan still worked for Wizards of the Coast, they did some awesome hands-on research at the GenCon D&D tables' and links the WotC article. Post dated 29 Sep 2013. Every limb supported.

claim: A 2025 EN World poster re-cites the 2005 Noonan/Decker WotC article: two sentences, 'DMs who didn't used boxed text had more engagement', cold reading is worse than personal phrasing, 'Ditch the boxed text and use your own words' — upstream article not fetched, single-lineage claim.
source: EN World — Read aloud text in modules: What are folks' opinions? (thread, page 4, 2025-04-05)
quote: Ditch the boxed text and use your own words

verdict.trueWording: Ditch the boxed text and use your own words
verdict.note: Post #37 by 'touc', Apr 5, 2025, on page 4. Verbatim on page: 'There's a 2005 WOTC article (archived in criteria comments, Dave Noonan & Jesse Decker)'; the two-sentence block quote; 'DMs who didn't used boxed text had more engagement' (reproduced with the source's own grammatical error); 'DMs with box text are reading it "cold," not having written it in their style nor practiced how it sounds'; and 'Ditch the boxed text and use your own words for the initial description of the room.' The claim's own self-flag stands: this is the forum re-citation, not the upstream WotC article, which I did not fetch.

claim: Thread posters set ceilings of 'no more than two sentences' (GM Lent) or '3 to 5 sentences at most' with listed details for closer investigation (el-remmen).
source: EN World — Read aloud text in modules: What are folks' opinions? (thread, page 4, 2025-04-05)
quote: 3 to 5 sentences at most

verdict.trueWording: 3 to 5 sentences at most and then other details listed
verdict.note: Both attributions correct on page 4. el-remmen (Moderator Emeritus, #34, Apr 5 2025): 'I find it useful if written well and concisely. 3 to 5 sentences at most and then other details listed to be shared if the party looks closer/investigates/interacts.' - designated quote verbatim, and the 'listed details for closer investigation' limb verbatim too. GM Lent (#31): 'boxed text shouldn't be more than two sentences' - the claim renders this as 'no more than two sentences', a paraphrase of identical meaning, not a verbatim quotation; the limb itself is supported.

claim: Shawn Merwin's D&D Beyond craft column: an opening should be 'Four sentences, and less than 100 words'; avoid 'paragraph after paragraph of boxed text'.
source: D&D Beyond — Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2019-11-06)
quote: Four sentences, and less than 100 words

verdict.trueWording: Four sentences, and less than 100 words.
verdict.note: By Shawn Merwin, Nov 6 2019, on dndbeyond.com. Both quoted strings verbatim: under the heading 'A Boxed-Text Opening' the column presents a four-sentence in-media-res opening and comments 'Four sentences, and less than 100 words.'; Tip 2 has 'Nothing slows a game more than paragraph after paragraph of boxed text'. Nuance recorded, not a downgrade: the 100-word figure is stated as a descriptive count of the column's own model opening rather than as an explicit 'should', though the column plainly holds it up as the standard to emulate.

claim: A 5e designer describes evolving from verbose 5e style to bullets to boxed text that is 'typically three lines, and never longer than five' because it sped play and set a base tone per room.
source: Revivify Games — What I Value In Adventure Design (2025-03-04)
quote: typically three lines, and never longer than five

verdict.trueWording: typically three lines, and never longer than five
verdict.note: Live host 403s a bare fetch and has no Wayback capture; reached raw on the www. host with full browser headers (HTTP 200). Page dated March 4, 2025. Every limb verbatim: 'the 5e work that I have done was longer form with bolded paragraph leaders and verbose descriptions'; 'So, I evolved and started to work toward the opposite side of the spectrum, focusing on short, bulleted phrases'; 'I introduced boxed text back into my typical formatting'; 'all my boxed text is precise... typically three lines, and never longer than five'; 'In practice, it has sped up play'; 'it allows me, as the designer, to help set a base-level tone for each room'.

claim: Sly Flourish: a read-aloud is a tiny story told in 'less than 250 words'; if editing didn't remove 25% you didn't try; 'Keep it short and keep it powerful.'
source: Sly Flourish — Writing Awesome Read-Aloud Text (Mike Shea, 2010-11-08)
quote: less than 250 words to tell it

verdict.trueWording: You have a tiny story to tell and less than 250 words
verdict.note: By Mike (Shea), 8 November 2010. All three fragments verbatim: 'writing good read-aloud text is like writing micro-fiction. You have a tiny story to tell and less than 250 words to tell it'; 'If you didn't edit your read-aloud text and remove 25% of what was there, you didn't try hard enough'; 'Keep it short and keep it powerful.' Every limb supported.

claim: Outside introductions, a boxed text with a paragraph break 'isn't already too long by half' is rare; villain dialogue should be broken into ~six-second (one-round) statements.
source: Dungeon Master's Workshop — DM 101: Mastering the Boxed Text (2019-09-27)
quote: isn't already too long by half

verdict.trueWording: Aside from introductory passages... too long by half
verdict.note: Under the heading 'Don't Overdo It': 'Aside from introductory passages, it's rare that a boxed text that includes a paragraph break isn't already too long by half. This is especially the case with villain appearances... consider breaking it into statements that can be made in about six seconds - the average length of a round - and drop the phrases in during the fight.' Designated quote verbatim; both limbs, including the six-second/one-round equivalence, verbatim.

claim: Bryce Lynch: long read-aloud at each location means 'the players are almost certainly going to be playing with their phones', even when, rarely, the prose is good.
source: tenfootpole.org — (5e) Death in the Wood review (Bryce Lynch, 2019-02-09)

verdict.trueWording: the players are almost certainly going to be playing with their phones
verdict.note: Bryce Lynch, '(5e) Death in the Wood', posted February 9, 2019. Body text verbatim: 'There's long read-aloud at the beginning of each location... It's also pretty well written, which I don't think I've said more than three or four times? It does a good job of communicating the social vibe going on. It's still too long and the players are almost certainly going to be playing with their phones, but it's not the overwritten fantasy drivil that is present in most read aloud.' The 'even when, rarely, the prose is good' limb is carried by 'pretty well written, which I don't think I've said more than three or four times'. Sentence is in the review body, not a comment.

feature: third person over second person in boxed text
claim: Merwin's core fix: 'Move from the second-person point of view to the third person' — 'The bloated corpse of a headless dragon dominates the center of this small clearing' instead of 'As you enter the clearing, you notice…' — so text cannot dictate PC actions or feelings.
source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
quote: Move from the second-person point of view to the third person

verdict.trueWording: Tip 1. Move from the second-person point of view to the third person.
verdict.note: Shawn Merwin, Critical Hits, August 27, 2010. Tip 1 heading verbatim. Both example strings verbatim and matching THIS 2010 version rather than the 2019 D&D Beyond rewrite: 'By avoiding the second-person ("As you enter the clearing, you notice the bloated corpse of a headless dragon") and using the third-person ("The bloated corpse of a headless dragon dominates the center of this small clearing")'. The 'actions or feelings' limb is supported in the essay body, not only by inference: 'boxed text can be rife with pitfalls when it assumes character feelings, movements, and actions.'

claim: Alexander names the pitfall 'remote-control text': 'You step forward', 'You smile', or declaring 'the thoughts or feelings' of PCs; show the scene, 'don't tell them how they're reacting to it'.
source: The Alexandrian — GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls (Justin Alexander, 2022-08-01)
quote: the thoughts or feelings

verdict.trueWording: declaring the thoughts or feelings or (worse yet!) actions of the PCs
verdict.note: All of this is Alexander's own essay body (above the comment section), unlike claim 101. Section heading 'REMOTE-CONTROL BOXED TEXT'; 'Remote-control boxed text suffers from similar problems (preventing the players from participating), but insidiously goes one step further by declaring the thoughts or feelings or (worse yet!) actions of the PCs'; the two bad examples '"You step forward and return the king's greeting with a deep bow."' and '"As you return to Waterdeep, you smile, thinking fondly of the ale at Trollskull Manor."'; and the cure 'Focus on showing the players the scene and letting them react to it. Don't tell them how they're reacting to it.' Only cosmetic drift: the page's term is 'remote-control boxed text' and the second example's 'you smile' is lowercase mid-sentence.

Long-time players tend to want bullet lists, bare bones text that allows them to improvise in response to the players at the table, a bit more wiggle room, less wall of text.' Save that for sourcebooks.' Quote verbatim; the PC-cannot-learn condition and the sourcebook destination are both explicit, and 'not adventures' is the column's subject.

claim: Hooks must be specific and hard to refuse; vague or cliched openings (stranger in a tavern, request from the mayor) fail.

Vague, overused, or clichéd hooks don't interest players because they have heard them before.' The overused list includes 'Meeting a stranger in a tavern' and 'Requests from the mayor or head villager'. Quote verbatim; every limb, including both cited examples, is on the page.

claim: Baur borrows fiction's inciting incident: an arrow with an Elvish note shot into camp beats a guy in a bar.

In fiction, it would be called the "inciting incident."' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported.

feature: design labels kept out of game text

claim: Greenwood says shared-world writers must fit in, perhaps even to a particular prose style, without contradicting existing lore.

Character descriptions, backstories, aims, and mannerisms are usually well-established, and the writer faces the daunting task of "fitting in" (perhaps even to a particular prose style) and not contradicting what may be a sizable body of existing lore.' Quote verbatim, speaker attribution explicit ('Greenwood:'), every limb supported.

claim: Greenwood writes by imagining he is present, smelling and tasting what characters do, then writing down enough for the reader to see the crypt or court.

I'm smelling what the characters are smelling, tasting what they're—well, you know the rest. What I then have to do is write down enough of what I can see, in my mind's eye, so that any reader will feel they too can see the moldering crypt ... or the glittering court of Zayang the Unimpeachable." Every limb — imagining presence, smelling, tasting, writing enough for the reader to see crypt and court — is on the page. Quote matches word for word (page uses a curly apostrophe).

claim: Crawford reads a rule first as written, in context and without regard to intent, because the published text must stand on its own.

Whenever I consider a rule, I start with this perspective." Reads-first, in-context, intent-disregarded and stands-on-its-own limbs all present.

feature: rules as foundation, DM as bridge

The direction we chose for the current edition was to lay a foundation of rules that a DM could build on, and we embraced the DM's role as the bridge between the things the rules address and the things they don't." Deliberateness ('the direction we chose') is explicit.

claim: Tone is gated by a Lord of the Rings / Game of Thrones plausibility test; humor and tragedy are allowed only if they do not overtake the general tone.

claim: Headings descend Chapter Title > Heading 1 > 2 > 3 > Inline Subhead without skipping, and exist for structure, never aesthetics.
