quote: Use a heading for a structural reason, not an aesthetic one

verdict.trueWording: Work down the hierarchy without skipping steps
verdict.note: p.3 'Headings': hierarchy printed as Chapter Title / Heading 1 / Heading 2 / Heading 3 / Inline Subhead [aka Heading 4], introduced by 'Work your way down the heading hierarchy without skipping steps'; then 'Use a heading for a structural reason, not an aesthetic one.' Quote verbatim; both limbs on the page.

claim: The inline subhead (heading 4) is set in bold italics and ends with a period, exclamation point, or question mark, not a colon.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: should be followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon

verdict.trueWording: Use a period, an exclamation point, or a question mark
verdict.note: p.3 'Inline Subheads': 'The lowest level of our heading hierarchy is the inline subhead. It functions as our heading 4. Contrary to past D&D usage, this subhead should be followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon. Use a period, an exclamation point, or a question mark.' Bold-italics limb: 'If you don't have access to the style, set the subhead in bold italics to distinguish it from text that is simply bold' (p.3), confirmed on p.4 ('the entire inline subhead is bold italics').

claim: American spelling and punctuation are house style, with Merriam-Webster's first-listed variant winning (toward, backward).
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: we use “toward,” not “towards,”

verdict.trueWording: we use “toward,” not “towards,”
verdict.note: Quote verbatim p.4 'Variant Spellings'. All limbs on page: 'We use American style for spelling and punctuation'; 'If a word has variants in Webster's, we use the one printed first (regardless of alphabetical order), except as noted in the D&D word list'; both examples toward/backward present. Merriam-Webster's Collegiate 11th named as a primary house resource on p.1.

claim: The serial (Oxford) comma is mandatory.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: We require the serial comma

verdict.trueWording: We require the serial comma
verdict.note: Quote verbatim p.4 under heading 'The Serial Comma'. 'Require' = mandatory; the Mystra/Elminster example shows the ambiguity rationale. '(Oxford)' in the claim is only a synonym for 'serial comma', not a separate assertion the page must carry.

claim: Negative contractions (don't, can't, wasn't) are encouraged; other contractions are used with care where they could be misread.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: We encourage the use of contractions formed with “not,”

verdict.trueWording: We encourage the use of contractions formed with “not,”
verdict.note: Quote verbatim p.4. Page continues 'such as "don't," "can't," and "wasn't" (see Chicago 5.105). Use other contractions with care, especially any contraction that can be misread.' Both limbs — negatives encouraged, others used with care where misreadable — are explicit.

claim: 'Non-' is hyphenated before fantasy races (non-elf, non-drow) but closed for 'nonhuman', and numeral-plus-abbreviation compounds are never hyphenated (100 gp treasure).
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: non-elf, non-dwarf

verdict.trueWording: non-elf, non-dwarf
verdict.note: Quote verbatim p.4. Page: 'The prefix is hyphenated in front of many of our fantasy races: non-elf, non-dwarf, non-orc, non-drow (but nonhuman, as in Webster's).' Numeral limb also explicit: 'we don't hyphenate a compound composed of a numeral and an abbreviation. So, it's a "100 gp treasure," not a "100-gp treasure."' The page's hedge 'many of our fantasy races' is exactly the nonhuman exception the claim itself carries.

claim: Possessives follow Chicago 17th edition (7.16–29), including names ending in an unpronounced s.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: We follow the approach in the seventeenth edition

verdict.trueWording: We follow the approach in the seventeenth edition
verdict.note: Quote verbatim p.4 under 'Possessives', followed on-page by '(see Chicago 7.16–29)'. The unpronounced-s limb is explicit: 'particularly those that involve words that end with an unpronounced s, as in "Descartes."'

feature: words used as words / foreign words
claim: English words used as words go in quotation marks; a non-English word, real or invented, is italicized when used as a word.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: is italicized when used as a word

verdict.trueWording: is italicized when used as a word
verdict.note: Quote verbatim p.4. English limb explicit: 'Our style for words used as words is to enclose them in quotes if the words are English (see Chicago 7.63).' 'real or invented' matches 'A non-English word, whether from the real world or a D&D world, is italicized when used as a word.'

claim: Vertical lists are introduced by a complete sentence ending in a colon, items start with a capital, and closing punctuation appears only if items are full sentences.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: introduce it with a complete sentence ending with a colon

verdict.trueWording: introduce it with a complete sentence ending with a colon
verdict.note: Quote verbatim p.4. Page scopes it to 'a bulleted list—or any other vertical list, such as a numbered one', and adds 'We begin each list item with a capital letter. Use closing punctuation in an item only if the list is composed of complete sentences.' All three limbs present.

claim: Whole numbers zero through one hundred are spelled out in prose (Chicago 9.2), with the usual exceptions for units, parts of a book, dates, and times.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: we spell out whole numbers from zero to one hundred

verdict.trueWording: we spell out whole numbers from zero to one hundred
verdict.note: Quote verbatim p.5, preceded by 'We follow the general rule for numerals that is presented in Chicago 9.2.' All four named exceptions appear in the page's bulleted exception list: units of measure {6'3", 5 gp, 3 lb.}, parts of a book {chapter 2, page 34, table 9}, dates, and times. 'In prose' is the page's own contrast: 'Numerals in Rules. In rules writing, we use numerals more often.'

claim: 'Percent' is written as a word except in tables or tight lists; percentile dice are 'd100', never 'd%'.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: Use the word “percent,” rather than the symbol %

verdict.trueWording: Use the word “percent,” rather than the symbol %
verdict.note: Quote verbatim p.5. Exception limb explicit: 'You can break this rule in a table, as well as in a list where space is tight.' Dice limb explicit: 'Also, the abbreviation we use for percentile dice is d100, not d%.'

claim: Cross-references are used judiciously; chapters are cited by number, subsections and sidebars by quoted title, tables by unquoted title.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: Use cross-references judiciously

verdict.trueWording: Use cross-references judiciously
verdict.note: Quote verbatim p.5 ('They are useful tools that can be easily overused'). Chapter limb p.5: 'When you refer to a chapter, use its number.' Subsection/sidebar and table limbs p.6: 'When you refer to a subsection, including a sidebar, use its title in quotes. A table title is not enclosed in quotes.'

claim: Appendices are lettered, not numbered, and cited like chapters ('see appendix A').
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: We use letters, not numbers, for appendices

verdict.trueWording: We use letters, not numbers, for appendices
verdict.note: Quote verbatim p.5. Cited-like-chapters limb explicit: 'References to appendices should follow the same principles that we follow for chapter references', with the on-page example '• See appendix A for definition of each condition.'

claim: Page references are avoided because they are hand-added at galley and break across reprints; cross-product page references are especially discouraged.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: We avoid page references as much as possible

verdict.trueWording: We avoid page references as much as possible
verdict.note: Quote verbatim, though it sits on p.6 of the PDF, not the p.5 the claim record cites — a locator slip, not a substance error. Both reasons on page: '(they must be added by hand during galley review), and they invite error'; and 'Referencing a particular page in another product is especially ill-advised; that product's pagination could change in a reprint or a new edition.'

claim: A character is 'on' a plane of existence but 'in' a plane named without the word 'plane' (in Elysium).
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: “She is in Elysium.”

verdict.trueWording: “She is in Elysium.”
verdict.note: Quote verbatim p.6 under 'Planes of Existence'. Both limbs explicit: 'A character is on a plane of existence. For example, "He was trapped on the Plane of Fire." But a character is in a plane when it is referred to by name without the word "plane."'

claim: Ability scores, action names, class features, feats, skills, languages, planes, and race/monster traits are capitalized as proper game terms.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: Action names {the Attack action, the Dash action}

verdict.trueWording: Action names {the Attack action, the Dash action}
verdict.note: Quote verbatim p.6 in the 'Terms to Capitalize' list. Every one of the eight categories the claim names is on that list: Ability scores {Strength, Intelligence}; Action names; Class features {Sneak Attack, Rage}; Feats {Loremaster}; Languages {Common, Dwarvish, Elvish}; Planes of existence {the Abyss, the Nine Hells}; Skills {Arcana, Perception}; Traits in races and monsters {Aquatic, Keen Senses}. Scoped on page to the RPG: 'In the RPG, certain terms receive special typographic treatment.'

claim: Spells, magic items, and artifacts are italicized and treated as titles, and the effect a spell creates is not italicized.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: Spells {magic missile}

verdict.trueWording: Terms to Italicize: Artifacts, Magic items, Spells {magic missile}
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.6 under 'Terms to Italicize' (artifacts, magic items, spells all listed). The second limb sits one page later, p.7: 'The italicized terms are treated as titles... Don't confuse one of these titles with an effect it creates (see Chicago 8.174). For example, the wall of fire spell produces a wall of fire, not a wall of fire (the latter would imply an infinite loop).' Both limbs supported; only the page cite (p.6) is narrow for the second limb.

claim: A stat block name is bolded in running text only at its first appearance in an encounter area, and nothing may sit between the number and the name.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: write “four goblins,” not “four loud goblins”

verdict.trueWording: Bold only first appearance; no text between number and stat block name
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.6. Both limbs explicit there: 'Set a monster's name in bold only the first time it appears in an encounter area or other subsection' and 'Make sure no text gets between the number of monsters appearing and the name of the stat block.'

claim: Rules prose uses numerals for points, damage, durations of game effects, and tactical distances, but spells out narrative quantities (six hours, fifty miles).
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: The two cities are fifty miles apart.

verdict.trueWording: Numerals for points, damage, game durations, tactical distances
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.7 under 'Numerals in Rules Text'. Every limb explicit: 'Use numerals for points, scores, damage expressions, and any game trait with a numerical value'; 'units of time that quantify the duration of a game effect'; 'units of distance that quantify the size or extent of game effects' plus 'dimensions and distances... on a tactical scale'. The narrative counterexamples are the guide's own: 'the characters slept for six hours' and 'The two cities are fifty miles apart.'

claim: The guide fixes verb-noun pairings: you cast a spell, take damage, make a saving throw, finish a rest, score a critical hit.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: You take damage.

verdict.trueWording: Verb Usage list: cast, take damage, make a saving throw, finish a rest
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.7. The 'Verb Usage' list carries all five pairings: 'You cast a spell.', 'You take damage.', 'You make a saving throw, and it succeeds or fails.', 'You finish a short or long rest.', 'You score a critical hit.' (guide's rest wording is 'a short or long rest').

claim: Rules must say 'succeed on a DC 15 check', not 'make a DC 15 check', unless the outcomes follow immediately.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: “You must succeed on a DC 15 Strength check

verdict.trueWording: Succeed on a DC 15 Strength check, not make one, unless outcomes follow
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.7 under 'Making a Roll vs. Succeeding on One'. The unless-clause is the guide's own: "Don't write, 'You must make a DC 15 Strength check...' unless that sentence is immediately followed by a description of what happens on a success or failure." Claim drops the ability name (Strength) but adds nothing.

claim: 'Save' for 'saving throw' is used sparingly, mainly in stat blocks; the 4E sense of 'save' as a successful saving throw is abandoned.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: use it sparingly, preferably only in a stat block

verdict.trueWording: Sparingly, preferably only in a stat block; 4E sense abandoned
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.7 under 'Saving Throws'. Both limbs explicit: 'use it sparingly, preferably only in a stat block or when preceded by "saving throw"' and 'In 4E, we used "save" as a synonym for "successful saving throw." We have abandoned that practice.' The claim omits the second permitted context (when preceded by 'saving throw'), which narrows rather than overstates.

claim: 'Result' no longer means the number on the die; it means the die roll plus modifiers, and 'total' is often preferred.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: We often prefer the word “total”

verdict.trueWording: Die-number sense abandoned; result = roll plus modifiers; total preferred
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.8 under '"Result" and Die Rolls'. All three limbs: 'In 3E and 4E, the word "result" was sometimes used as a synonym for "the number rolled on a die." We have abandoned that practice'; '"Result" can legitimately refer to the sum of a die roll and any modifiers'; 'We often prefer the word "total" in such a context.'

claim: Damage is written as '10 fire damage', never '10 points of fire damage'.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: Avoid referring to points of damage

verdict.trueWording: Avoid points of damage: write 10 fire damage, not 10 points of fire damage
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.8 under 'Points of Damage'. The guide's example is the claim verbatim: 'write, "The spell deals 10 fire damage," not "The spell deals 10 points of fire damage."' Claim's 'never' hardens the heading verb 'Avoid', but the worked example is a flat write-X-not-Y.

claim: The die expression stays with the damage type: 'an extra 1d4 fire damage'.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: We write “an extra 1d4 fire damage,”

verdict.trueWording: We like to keep the die expression with the damage type
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.8 under 'Extra Damage'. Rationale limb explicit: 'We write "an extra 1d4 fire damage," not "1d4 extra fire damage." We like to keep the die expression with the damage type.'

claim: One is proficient 'in' a skill, language, or activity but 'with' a tool, weapon, or armor.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: proficient in Elvish and Arcana

verdict.trueWording: Proficient in a skill/language/activity; with a tool/weapon/armor
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.8 under 'Proficiency'. Both bullets match limb for limb: 'proficient... in a skill, language, or other activity that is learnable and repeatable' and 'proficient... with a tool, weapon, type of armor, or other object', with the example 'proficient in Elvish and Arcana... proficient with longswords and heavy armor.'

claim: 'Dungeon Master' is never a verb except in conversational web writing.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: This term is a noun, not a verb

verdict.trueWording: Noun not verb; breakable in an informal context such as a blog
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.8 under '"Dungeon Master" Isn't a Verb'. The exception in the source is broader than the claim's: 'This rule can be broken in an informal context, such as in a blog or a web article that has a conversational tone' — informal context generally, with blog/web article as examples. The claim is stricter than the guide, not unsupported.

feature: weeks and months banned in rules
claim: Because week and month lengths vary by world (a Realms week is a tenday), rules durations are given in days or years, never weeks or months.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: say a game effect lasts for 7 days, not 1 week

verdict.trueWording: Week is ten days in the Realms, a tenday; use days, years allowed
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.8 under 'Avoid "Week" and "Month"'. Every limb: 'The lengths of weeks and months vary in different D&D worlds. A week is ten days long in the Forgotten Realms, for instance, and is called a tenday'; "don't express durations or other lengths of time in weeks or months when you're writing rules"; 'The length of the year varies as well, but you may use years for durations and the like.'

claim: 'Human' is not a synonym for 'mortal', and 'humanoid' is used cautiously because it names a creature type.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: Beware of using “human” as a synonym for “mortal.”

verdict.trueWording: Beware human for mortal; be cautious with humanoid, a creature type
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.8 under 'Misusing "Human" and "Humanoid"'. Second limb explicit: 'be cautious when using the word "humanoid," given the fact that it refers to a creature type. For example, a giant has humanlike features, but it isn't a humanoid in the game.'

claim: A word list fixes spellings and plurals: dwarves not dwarfs, mithral not mithril, staffs, war band, drow/kenku/yuan-ti unchanged in plural.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: mithral (not mithril)

verdict.trueWording: Word list: dwarves (not dwarfs), mithral (not mithril), staffs, war band
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.9. Every listed item found in the same word list on p.9: 'dwarves (not dwarfs)', 'mithral (not mithril)', 'staffs', 'war band (not warband)', 'drow (singular and plural)', 'kenku (singular and plural)', 'yuan-ti (singular and plural)'.

feature: Forgotten Realms terms in the general guide
claim: The general guide carries a short Realms list: Goodman/Goodwoman capped, 'goodsir' lowercased, 'godsforsaken' as the Realms form of godforsaken, and 'the Realms' only after 'the Forgotten Realms'.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: goodsir (a form of address, not capped)

verdict.trueWording: goodsir (a form of address, not capped)
verdict.note: Raw PDF text extracted (pdfminer + pypdf). p.9 'Forgotten Realms Terms' list carries verbatim 'Goodman/Goodwoman (a title or form of address, usu. capped)', 'godsforsaken (established in the Realms...)', 'goodsir (a form of address, not capped)'; the list continues on p.10 with 'the Realms (should be preceded by “the Forgotten Realms”)'. All four limbs supported. Only hedge: source says 'usu. capped', claim says 'capped'.

claim: 'Godsforsaken' is the established Realms form but is not required in other polytheistic settings, since 'godforsaken' has no necessary monotheistic sense.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: godsforsaken (established in the Realms

verdict.trueWording: godsforsaken (established in the Realms, but not necessary in other polytheistic settings; “godforsaken” has no necessary connection to monotheism)
verdict.note: Quote fragment appears word for word on p.9 of the v1.08a PDF; every limb of the claim (established Realms form, not necessary elsewhere, godforsaken has no necessary monotheistic connection) is the source's own wording.

claim: 'Fellowship' is avoided for a party because of its Tolkien association and because D&D parties are often fractious or mercenary; 'party', 'group', 'band', or 'company' are preferred.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: use “group,” “band,” “company,” or, especially, “party.”

verdict.trueWording: use “group,” “band,” “company,” or, especially, “party.”
verdict.note: p.9 'Adventuring Parties' sidebar, verbatim: 'The word “fellowship” has strong connections with The Lord of the Rings and doesn’t represent the typical D&D adventuring party well... D&D adventuring companies are often fractious or more mercenary than the word “fellowship” implies. In most in-world contexts and all other contexts, use “group,” “band,” “company,” or, especially, “party.”' All three limbs (Tolkien association, fractious/mercenary, four preferred words) supported.

claim: Standard abbreviations are fixed (PH, DMG, MM, gp, d100, AC, DC, DM, XP, HD, hp, NPC).
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: NPC nonplayer character

verdict.trueWording: NPC nonplayer character
verdict.note: pypdf page-10 reconstruction gives the table row verbatim: 'HD Hit Die/Dice \n hp hit points \n NPC nonplayer character'. Every abbreviation named in the claim is present in the p.10 Abbreviations tables: PH, DMG, MM (Brand/Product), gp (Coin), d100 (Die), AC, DC, DM, XP, HD, hp, NPC (Other Term).

claim: The superseded 2013 guide banned singular they outside informal contexts like dialogue.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (2013)
quote: Don’t use “they” or “their” as singular pronouns

verdict.trueWording: Don’t use “they” or “their” as singular pronouns, except in an informal context like dialogue.
verdict.note: v1.04a PDF confirmed (footer 'Version 1.04a ©2013 Wizards of the Coast'); quote is verbatim on p.2 under 'Achieving Gender Neutrality'. Both limbs (ban; informal-context/dialogue exception) supported.

claim: The 2013 guide framed gender neutrality as assuming a readership of both men and women, a framing dropped in 2019 for 'we don't assume a gender identity'.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (2013)
quote: readership includes both men and women

verdict.trueWording: We also assume that our readership includes both men and women.
verdict.note: Quote verbatim on p.2 of v1.04a. The second limb checks out against v1.08a: the 2019 guide has zero occurrences of 'readership' and its Gender section instead reads 'We don’t assume that our readers are of a particular gender identity.' Note the claim's inline rendering 'we don’t assume a gender identity' is a compression, not the 2019 wording.

feature: existence of a post-2019 house style guide
claim: A Word version of the house style guide, authored by Kim Mohan and last modified by Judy Bauer on 2021-07-06 at Wizards of the Coast, ships inside the Dungeoncraft Pack (2023-12-04) and postdates the public v1.08a PDF.
source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04

verdict.trueWording: creator Kim Mohan; lastModifiedBy 'Bauer, Judy'; modified 2021-07-06; Company Wizards of the Coast.
verdict.note: Zip fetched (HTTP 200, 1,624,152 bytes) and expanded; 'Dungeoncraft Pack/DnD House Style Guide.docx' present, zip entry dated 12-04-2023 matching the pack URL. docProps/core.xml verbatim: <dc:creator>Kim Mohan</dc:creator>, <cp:lastModifiedBy>Bauer, Judy</cp:lastModifiedBy>, <dcterms:created>2016-03-07T20:43:00Z</dcterms:created>, <dcterms:modified>2021-07-06T18:09:00Z</dcterms:modified>; docProps/app.xml <Company>Wizards of the Coast</Company>. 2021-07-06 postdates the v1.08a PDF (©2018, 'updated January 2019'). Empty quote field, so graded on substance.

claim: The 2021 docx cites merriam-webster.com rather than the printed 11th edition Collegiate.
source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
quote: merriam-webster.com

verdict.trueWording: merriam-webster.com
verdict.note: docx body line 5, in the two-primary-resources list: 'The Chicago Manual of Style, 17th edition / merriam-webster.com'. The contrast limb holds: the docx has zero occurrences of 'Collegiate', while v1.08a p.1 reads 'Merriam-Webster’s Collegiate Dictionary, 11th edition'.

claim: The 2021 docx reverses the 2019 rule: 'man' and 'woman' may now describe the gender of any people, so 'dwarf man' and 'gnome woman' are fine.
source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
quote: we can write “dwarf man” or “gnome woman.”

verdict.trueWording: we can write “dwarf man” or “gnome woman.”
verdict.note: docx 'Gender and Fantasy Races': '“Man,” “woman,” and their plurals are fine for describing the gender of people. For example, we can write “dwarf man” or “gnome woman.”' The reversal limb is confirmed against v1.08a p.2, which reads 'reserved for describing humans only. For example, we write “male dwarf,” not “dwarf man” or “man dwarf.”' — the exact phrase the docx now permits.

claim: The 2021 docx allows they/their/them/themself for a person of unknown gender without the 2019 'don't abuse this liberty' caveat, requiring only a clear antecedent.
source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
quote: you must ensure that the pronoun’s antecedent is clear

verdict.trueWording: you must ensure that the pronoun’s antecedent is clear
verdict.note: docx: 'We allow the use of “they,” “their,” “them,” and “themself” when referring to a person whose gender is unknown. But you must ensure that the pronoun’s antecedent is clear if more than one person appears in the context.' All four pronouns present; docx has zero occurrences of 'abuse this liberty', which v1.08a carries ('but don’t abuse this liberty. Rely on this device only when you have no other reasonable or pleasing alternative').

claim: In running text a person's preferred pronoun (he, she, or they) is used; in rules text 'it' is used.
source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
quote: In rules text, use “it.”

verdict.trueWording: In rules text, use “it.”
verdict.note: docx 'Pronoun Preference' — 'Short Version: In running text, use a person’s preferred pronoun: he, she, or they. Whatever pronoun you use, ensure that its antecedent is clear. In rules text, use “it.”' Both limbs verbatim.

claim: Descriptive text uses they/them for Humanoids and other sapient creatures of unknown gender (including vampires), and 'it' for animals, cosmic horrors, and extraplanar creatures.
source: DnD House Style Guide.docx (Wizards of the Coast; created Kim Mohan 2016-03-07, last modified Judy Bauer 2021-07-06) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04

claim: Shawn Merwin's first rule for boxed text is to move from second person to third, and he supplies the same clearing in both, the third-person version making the corpse the subject.

Same clearing given both ways: second person 'As you enter the clearing, you notice the bloated corpse of a headless dragon'; third person 'The bloated corpse of a headless dragon dominates the center of this small clearing.' Quote verbatim; the corpse is the grammatical subject of the third-person version.

Quote verbatim; writer-and-editor limb ('when writing or editing') and the interaction limb both supported. (The later D&D Beyond rewrite reads 'when the PCs must interact with them on some level'; the quote as given matches the Critical Hits original cited.)

claim: Merwin's own model opening boxed text, printed in the article, is four sentences and under a hundred words, and he then explains what each of the four sentences does.

claim: Merwin tells adventure writers to avoid 'seems to be' and 'appears to be' in read-aloud text because for the characters perception is reality and the hedge invites metagaming.

verdict.trueWording: Tip 4 "Avoid 'seems to be' or 'appears to be.' For the characters, perception is reality."
verdict.note: dndbeyond.com Tip 4 heading is exactly 'Avoid “seems to be” or “appears to be.”' and the body opens 'For the characters, perception is reality.' and adds 'nothing triggers meta-gaming like the words “seems” or “appears” in boxed text.' Quote verbatim; the metagaming limb supported.

claim: Merwin makes reading boxed text aloud a required check, naming tongue-twisters and unintended alliteration as faults invisible on the page.

verdict.trueWording: "tongue-twisters, funny-sounding phrases, unintended alliteration... hard to spot on the page"

Trouble areas like tongue-twisters, funny-sounding phrases, unintended alliteration, and other pitfalls are hard to spot on the page but easy to hear when spoken.' Quote verbatim (hyphenated 'funny-sounding' matches the D&D Beyond text; the 2010 Critical Hits original reads 'funny sounding'). 'Required check' and 'invisible on the page' limbs supported.

claim: Merwin tells writers not to use game-mechanical words such as stunned or frightened in their ordinary sense inside read-aloud text.

verdict.trueWording: Tip 6 "Avoid game mechanical terms used in a non-mechanical way"; list includes stunned, frightened
verdict.note: dndbeyond.com Tip 6 heading verbatim; body: 'Terms like reaction, action, incapacitated, stunned, frightened, magical, and many others have specific meanings in the game. Using their normal connotations in proximity to mechanical bits can lead to confusion. Avoid them whenever possible.' The tip sits in the article's list of tips for boxed (read-aloud) text; every limb supported.

claim: Merwin says writing good boxed text needs the precision of fiction or poetry while also doing the work of technical writing.

verdict.trueWording: "It requires the same precision that one might use for fiction or poetry... much like technical writing."
verdict.note: dndbeyond.com opening: 'Writing good boxed text is difficult. It requires the same precision that one might use for fiction or poetry, while also trying to perform the mechanical task of dealing with game elements, much like technical writing.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported.

Minor paraphrase drift: the page says 'little to add', the claim says 'nothing to add' — the empty-closet sentence carries the stronger sense, so not scored down.

If the player characters meet the sheriff about a wanted poster, no one needs an item-by-item inventory of her kitchen.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported.

claim: Hartlage says Curse of Strahd gives pages of room description to notable NPCs' homes and calls Chris Perkins's details creepy and moody while judging most of those rooms unreachable in play.

claim: Justin Alexander's judgment on the state of the form is that published adventures' location keys are almost all bad.

claim: Alexander says a standardised section format pushes writers to fill every heading, so a Tactics section gets paragraphs even when the orcs have only swords.

The orc limb is the very next sentence: “You probably don’t really need to tell a DM that the orcs attack people using their swords (since that’s the only weapon they have)… but the format says you should have a ‘Tactics’ section, so you might as well write two or three paragraphs about it.” Under the ADVENTURE FORMATTING GUIDES heading, as cited.

claim: Alexander makes the order of a location description depend on the scene rather than a fixed template, contrasting a visible ogre with a hidden goblin.

quote: A room with an ogre standing in the middle of it

claim: Alexander dates the arrival of boxed text to Lost Tamoachan and says the prewritten descriptions appeared between quotation marks before TSR boxed them in the 1980 reissue.

claim: Bryce Lynch diagnoses Lost Mine of Phandelver's generic feel as a failure of modifiers rather than of nouns and verbs.

claim: Lynch shows the cure as a single added modifier before a role noun and lists six alternatives that would each conjure a different woman.

verdict.note: Verbatim: “‘The farmers wife tells you … ’ instead of the ‘the prim farmers wife tells you …’”. Six alternatives counted on the page: “Granny, prim, biddy, lusty, stoic, proper”, of which the page says “They conjure a NON-generic image in your mind that you can build on” — the claim’s “each conjure a different woman” is that in other words.

claim: Lynch's complaint about the Phandalin section is that the town's language is thin outside its core locations.

verdict.note: Verbatim inside “The whole town is quite light on descriptive and evocative language/scenes outside of the core locations”, in the Part 2 town section as cited. Lynch immediately widens it — “(and, I will assert later, IN the core locations as well.)” — so the claim is narrower than the page, not at odds with it.

claim: Lynch calls the one-sentence-per-NPC summary of who is in town, where they are and what they want invaluable and asks for more adventures to carry one.

That’s done in just a sentence or so each. I find these sorts of references INVALUABLE. … More adventures need to do this.”

verdict.note: Verbatim, and inside the “On to the bad” section as cited (heading two paragraphs above). Page: “The read-aloud in this, in many places, is laughable”, then single-sentence examples — “You stumble upon an old grave.”, “You find a corpse.” — culminating in “Here’s a masterpiece of creative read-aloud writing!!! ‘You find something on the ground.’”, which names nothing.

claim: Lynch credits Curse of Strahd with villages whose residents each have something going on, and says events attached to locations are what make the places feel alive.

Each with their own personality.” Events limb: “This is then augmented by many of the locations having events… almost every location has one or two events… It brings the place to life. No longer static many of the villages now feel alive…”

claim: The EN World column's fourth writing step is a halving target for every description, and it names adjectives and adverbs as the writer's enemies.
source: Radiating Gnome, EN World column
quote: those words are actually our mortal enemies

verdict.trueWording: those words are actually our mortal enemies
verdict.note: Raw thread page fetched with a browser UA (HTTP 200). Under '1. Write A Good Description' the 'Try this:' procedure's fourth bullet is 'Try to cut out half the words... We may not be able to cut out half of them, but make it a goal', and the same bullet reads 'When we write, we include modifiers -- adjective and adverbs -- and those words are actually our mortal enemies.' Quote exact. Note the article's own top-level step 4 is 'Delivery: Don't Read - Perform'; the halving is the fourth step of the WRITING procedure (Dausuul labels it 'D' in reply #5), which is what the claim says.

claim: The same column argues one well-chosen physical detail can stand for a whole person, instancing the loose skin under an old woman's arm.
source: Radiating Gnome, EN World column
quote: it paints a vivid image in your mind of the whole woman

verdict.trueWording: a flap of skin flaps under an old woman's arm
verdict.note: Same page, same section: 'if I describe the way a flap of skin flaps under an old woman's arm, it paints a vivid image in your mind of the whole woman, very quickly.' Quote exact. Standing-for-the-whole limb also carried by 'we can say a lot about a scene with one or two well-chosen details' and 'What's the one thing you can describe about a person or a place that will carry with it enough detail of the whole?' The claim's 'loose skin' is a gloss of the page's 'flap of skin', which is description, not quotation.

claim: A forum reader rewriting a Bastion of Broken Souls boxed text cuts the phrase 'appears as', calling the hedge a DM reflex the players do not need.

quote: "Appears as" is just instinctive DM pedantry

verdict.trueWording: instinctive DM pedantry... This is unnecessary. Players know about illusions.
verdict.note: Post #5 by Dausuul, dated Jul 15, 2013 on the page (matches the claim's attribution and date), rewriting boxed text from 'Bastion of Broken Souls'. Step D reads: '"Appears as" is just instinctive DM pedantry--hey, it could be an illusion, so I have to qualify that it "appears" this way. This is unnecessary. Players know about illusions.' The phrase is duly cut: the revision reads 'It's a python from the waist down.' Quote exact, every limb supported.

claim: The same reader deletes 'scaly' from the official description on the ground that the noun already carries it.

verdict.trueWording: When was the last time you met a snake that wasn't scaly?
verdict.note: Same post #5, same step D: 'Scaliness was pure fluff from the start. When was the last time you met a snake that wasn't scaly?' Quote exact. The 'noun already carries it' limb is the page's own reasoning — snakes are inherently scaly, and one sentence earlier 'by choosing "python" to replace "snake," we have already implied bigness, color, and coils, so we can cut those.' The source description is the official one from Bastion of Broken Souls, quoted on the page.

claim: Radiating Gnome rewrites an 81-word location description from Dungeon 213 down to 23 words and prints both side by side.

(from page 40, encounter area 2, Approach)'; he calls it 'one of the descriptions of a location'. He then writes 'Here are the two -- the original and my revision -- side by side' followed by a two-cell table, and closes 'That's 23 words verses the originals 81.' (typo 'verses' is the page's). Quote exact; all limbs on the page.

claim: In that rewrite he replaces the causeway's 'rising' with a climbing verb because rising suggests effortless floating.
source: Radiating Gnome, EN World
quote: the ramp needs to climb

verdict.trueWording: the ramp needs to climb, not rise. Rise sounds like floating up effortlessly
verdict.note: Post #6: '"rising like a ramp out of the island's bedrock" ... "rising" isn't my first choice here. We want to give the sense of the cliff and fortress above, the ramp needs to climb, not rise. Rise sounds like you're floating up effortlessly.' The replacement is executed in the final version: 'A lone craggy causeway climbs from island bedrock...'. Quote exact; the causeway is the subject; the effortless-floating rationale is verbatim on the page.

claim: He keeps an alliteration on purpose, saying the paired sound will stay in the listener's ear.
source: Radiating Gnome, EN World
quote: which will resonate in the listener's ear
confidence: medium — sits beside Merwin's opposite rule that unintended alliteration is a fault; the two are about intent, not sound

verdict.trueWording: the alliterative 'craggy causeway' which will resonate in the listener's ear
verdict.note: Post #6: 'Stone is probably not necessary... And that gives us the alliterative "craggy causeway" which will resonate in the listener's ear.' Quote exact. He keeps it deliberately — 'craggy causeway' survives into both revisions — and later reinforces the sound argument: 'it bring's the "c" sounds in from the beginning of the passage.' Strictly the alliteration is produced by cutting 'stone' as much as kept, but the deliberateness limb holds.

claim: He traces the reader's eye through the original passage from feet to cliff to causeway and back, and moves the load-bearing detail forward because listeners are lost after a sentence or two.
source: Radiating Gnome, EN World
quote: That seems like a lot of redirection

verdict.trueWording: down (feet) to up (cliff)... That seems like a lot of redirection
verdict.note: Post #6 traces it explicitly: 'the reader's attention is going from down (feet) to up (cliff) to up (stronghold) to up (battlements) jump all the way down (causeway) to up (stronghold) to down (tower). That seems like a lot of redirection -- putting the causeway and the tower much earlier in the description also evens out that progression a bit.' Quote exact. The listener-loss limb is on the same page a few paragraphs up: the tower 'is buried in the description. Assuming you lose listeners after the first or second sentence of reading this...' — note the two rationales sit in separate paragraphs (redirection/evenness here, listener-loss there), but both are the page's.

claim: Gus L. reads a one-line box of read-aloud text in Lost Mine of Phandelver as a symptom of an outdated house style rather than of that scene.

claim: Gus L. contrasts the bare category word for a monster with a specific physical description he writes out, arguing the second makes a mystery of the same creature.
source: Gus L., Dungeon of Signs
quote: is a mystery to be unraveled

verdict.trueWording: A 'goblin' is a vaguely defined monster... is a mystery to be unraveled
verdict.note: Description section: 'A "goblin" is a vaguely defined monster that low level adventurers are supposed to kill. A "4' tall thing with mottled white and lavender skin, vague drooping features, four ropy, ill matched limbs and a musty fungal odor" is a mystery to be unraveled.' Quote exact. Both halves describe the same creature (a goblin), and the surrounding text supplies the argument: 'monsters are reduced to ever more boring cliches if their only description is a name from a monster guide.'

claim: David Hartlage's example of boxed text failing is a 2012 tournament room whose load-bearing runes were listed among unimportant details and missed by his whole team.
source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon – boxed text', DMDavid
quote: the text mentioned the runes alongside other, less important details

verdict.trueWording: the text mentioned the runes alongside other, less important details
verdict.note: Raw dmdavid.com tag page carries the full post 'Picturing the dungeon - boxed text' (David Hartlage, November 15, 2012). 'In 2012, the final challenge required you to close six arcane gates while demons poured out... the DM dutifully read the boxed text, which included a description of mysterious runes on the pillars in the room. Like any good boxed text description, the text mentioned the runes alongside other, less important details. No one on my team appreciated the runes significance, so we failed to discover that disabling the runes reduced the extremely difficult arcana checks required to close the gates.' Quote exact; year, tournament (D&D Championship at GEN CON), room, load-bearing runes and whole-team miss all supported. One nuance short of a downgrade: Hartlage frames the text as 'any good boxed text description' and adds 'We could not blame the DM's wording, because every team heard the same boxed text' — so it is a failure of the form's information order, not one he pins on that DM's phrasing.

claim: Hartlage attributes boxed text's drag to delivery: a reader's voice takes a different tone and cadence from speech, and the monotony loses the listener.
source: David Hartlage, DMDavid
quote: their voice takes a different tone and cadence

verdict.trueWording: their voice takes a different tone and cadence than when they speak extemporaneously
verdict.note: Same post: 'Boxed text does have a drawback. When most speakers read something aloud, their voice takes a different tone and cadence than when they speak extemporaneously, and that monotony can cause players' attention to wander.' Quote exact; delivery-as-cause and monotony-loses-the-listener are the same sentence. He offers a second, content-side cause immediately after ('too many boxed text descriptions have lingered on... obviously unimportant fluff'), which does not contradict the claim.

claim: Hartlage, though he paraphrases at the table, says nothing has replaced boxed text as a way of summarising what players must learn on entering a room.
source: David Hartlage, DMDavid
quote: No one has shown a better way to summarize

verdict.trueWording: No one has shown a better way to summarize what the players must learn when they enter a room.
verdict.note: Same raw page. Quote verbatim. The paraphrase limb is also there two sentences earlier: 'when I know the content well enough, I paraphrase boxed text. Still, even for DMs who never read boxed text, it helps.'

'No description' is supported by the quoted line itself plus 'most of the original information ... is actually contained in the NPC write-up of its proprietor'.

claim: Alexander quotes Ruins of Undermountain (1991) declining to describe the inn on the stated ground of leaving DMs free rein, and calls the claim implausible given three prior books.

Sure. Whatever you say, TSR.

claim: Alexander records that City of Splendors (1994) fixes the inn's founding year and building class, adding registry-style facts to the accumulated description.
